title: Shockheyoune
summary: Shockheyoune appears in deed language for a swamp and creek at the Nissequogue River mouth. Its location on the west side of the river connects the name to shoreline, wetland, and boundary records along Long Island Sound.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Nissequogue Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: When Richard Smith Sr. transferred one hundred acres of land near the Nissequogue River to his son in 1676, he specifically used the Algonquian name Shockheyoune to identify the bordering swamp creek. The reliance on such Indigenous landmarks in early English family deeds highlights how completely Native geography structured the early colonial division and ownership of Long Island.
history_content: The name appears in a Smithtown deed for land and meadow near the Nissequogue River mouth. The modern marker is a general west-side river-mouth placement, not an exact creek boundary.
translation_content:
No secure derivation is given for Shockheyoune, so the meaning remains uncertain.

Why Place Names Matter

“Place-names weave a cultural understanding of the land into the land itself.”

— Lisa Prosper, The Language of Indigenous Heritage (2022), PDF page 7
preservation_content: Shockheyoune preserves a local creek and swamp name from the Nissequogue River mouth, where shoreline, meadow, and family land records overlap.
